why.headline: One strong leg launches every dive, to either side.

claims.text: You push off one leg to dive. In elite adult keepers, weaker-side dives moved slower toward the ball.
With one-leg training, older teen players evened out their two legs. Coaches of young players favour one-leg work.
In studies of adult keepers, saves were few but explosive. Many were dives and jumps.
Boys in their early teens did strength training twice weekly. After 6 weeks, long jumps were 1.1 to 6% longer. Adding jumps gave the bigger gain.
Early-teen players added five moves, one a single-leg squat, 4 times weekly. After 26 weeks, jumps were 5 to 6.8% higher.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

The muscle on the side of your hip
The muscles at the back of your thighs

note.text: Lunge studies measured these muscles in adults; none measured them in teens.

claims.text: In a study with adults, the lunge worked the front thigh hard. That level suits building leg strength.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested the split squat alone in goalkeepers. The youth trials mixed several exercises.
